source_text: Quodam die in diebus sanctis octauarum, cum mane apud me fuissent multi fratres laici christiani et in loco solito consedissemus, ortus est sermo de religione christiana aduersus praesumptionem et tamquam miram et magnam scientiam paganorum: quem recordatum atque conpletum litteris mandandum putaui non expressis personis contradicentium, quamuis christiani essent et magis contradicendo quaerere uiderentur, quid paganis responderi oporteret. cum ergo de diuinatione daemonum quaereretur et affirmaretur praedixisse nescio quem euersionem templi Serapis, quae in Alexandria facta est, respondi non esse mirandum, si istam euersionem templis et simulacris suis inminere daemones et scire et praedicere potuerunt sicut alia multa, quantum eis nosse et praenuntiare permittitur.
orientation: Augustine is introducing the occasion: during the octave days, Christian laymen gathered with him and began discussing Christian religion against pagan claims, which led to the question about demons predicting the destruction of the temple of Serapis.
pass_a_gloss: On a certain day in the holy days of the octaves, when in the morning many lay Christian brothers had been with me and we had sat down in the usual place, a discussion arose about the Christian religion against the presumption and as it were the wonderful and great knowledge of the pagans: which discussion, having remembered it and completed it, I thought should be committed to writing, without expressing the persons of those contradicting, although they were Christians and seemed rather by contradicting to be seeking what ought to be replied to the pagans. When therefore there was inquiry about the divination of demons and it was asserted that some person or other had predicted the overthrow of the temple of Serapis, which was done in Alexandria, I replied that it was not to be wondered at, if the demons were able both to know and to predict that this overthrow was threatening their temples and idols, just as many other things, as far as it is permitted to them to know and to foretell.

choices.english: in the holy days of the octaves
choices.why: Keeps the liturgical sense of the days following a feast, matching the source's 'diebus sanctis octauarum'.
Preserves the word order and the distinction 'laici' (lay) modifying 'fratres'.

choices.term: praesumptionem et tamquam miram et magnam scientiam paganorum
choices.english: the presumption and as it were the wonderful and great knowledge of the pagans
choices.why: Renders 'tamquam' as 'as it were' to keep the distancing nuance Augustine gives to pagan knowledge.
rejected: the presumption and the supposedly wonderful and great knowledge
the presumption and what seemed the wonderful and great knowledge

choices.english: without expressing the persons of those contradicting
choices.why: Keeps the ablative absolute literally and the participial force of 'contradicentium'.
rejected: without identifying the persons who contradicted

choices.english: some person or other had predicted
choices.why: Renders the indefinite 'nescio quem' with its dismissive tone.
Keeps the sense of impending danger inherent in 'inminere'.

pass_b_english: One day during the holy days of the octaves, when many lay Christian brothers had been with me in the morning and we had sat down in our usual place, a discussion arose about the Christian religion, set against the presumption and the supposedly wonderful and great knowledge of the pagans. I thought this discussion, once remembered and completed, should be committed to writing, without naming the persons who raised objections—though they were Christians and seemed to be asking, more by way of contradiction, what ought to be answered to pagans. So when the question of the divination of demons came up, and it was asserted that some person or other had predicted the overthrow of the temple of Serapis, which took place in Alexandria, I answered that it was not surprising if the demons were able both to know and to predict that this overthrow was threatening their temples and idols, just as they can know and foretell many other things, to the extent that they are permitted.

last_rejected.why: "Nescio quis" means "someone, I know not who"—the demon, not a human. The English suggests a human predictor.
last_rejected.fix: some demon or other had predicted
last_rejected.ruling: 'Nescio quem' = 'someone, I know not who'; context doesn't specify demon. 'Some person' is acceptable.

last_rejected.quote: that this overthrow was threatening their temples and idols
last_rejected.source_quote: istam euersionem templis et simulacris suis inminere
last_rejected.why: The overthrow threatens (is imminent to) their temples, not 'was threatening' as ongoing; also 'istam' = 'that' (the Serapeum's), not 'this'.
last_rejected.fix: that that overthrow threatened their temples and idols
last_rejected.ruling: 'inminere' = 'threaten'; 'was threatening' is valid. 'istam' as 'this' vs 'that' is minor preference.
